title: 395. I Dont Even Know If I Like You Yet https://www.thebestleadershipnewsletter.com/p/i-dont-even-know-if-i-like-you-not-getting-referrals
author: Jeff Matlow
source: The Best Leadership Newsletter Ever (thebestleadershipnewsletter.com), November 9, 2026
summary: Jeff Matlow argues that asking someone you have just met for referrals or client introductions is a bad sales habit, because it asks them to risk their own reputation for a stranger. He opens with a first-date-marriage-proposal analogy, then explains that a referral tells a trusting contact that they should trust you too. Liking someone is not the same as trusting them, and trust is earned through reliability shown over time rather than requested in a single call. His own practice is to offer something useful after a first conversation, such as an article or an idea, and to keep building the relationship without expecting anything back. The recommended ask is for perspective or a second conversation, so that the risk of working with you shrinks until referrals feel like an opportunity. The tone is irreverent and the message is practical for any leader who builds a network.
points: A referral lends your reputation to a stranger, so asking for one early asks the other person to take a risk, not to help.
Liking someone and trusting them are different, and trust comes from demonstrated follow-through after the first meeting.
Build the relationship in the weeks after a call by sharing useful articles and ideas, without expecting anything in return.
Ask for a perspective or a second conversation instead, and focus on making a great second impression.
quotes: You’re not asking them for help. What you’re doing is asking them to take a risk.
They’re telling that person who trusts them that they should also trust you. They’re putting their reputation on the line.
Liking you isn’t the same as trusting you. I might think you’re smart, funny, and fascinating. We might have a wonderful conversation.
Trust isn’t just about whether I like you. It’s about whether I know you well enough to stop worrying that you’re going to screw things up.
I’m just building a relationship. There’s a big difference there. Because trust isn’t built during a single 30-minute Zoom call. It’s built through what happens after the call.
Ask for their perspective on something you’re working on. Ask if they’d be open to having another discussion.
You don’t get referrals by convincing people to take a risk on you. You get referrals by making that risk smaller.
So stop worrying about making a great first impression, focus on making a great second impression.
